prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms are interrogated at a magic wavelength free of lattice light shifts, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: I keep B051 alone, with Katori and Ye. After round 1 the case has not weakened. No member disputes the measurement itself: the 1e-18 systematic uncertainty and the stability are reproduced by independent laboratories and by clock-to-clock links, which is the kind of evidence I weight most. The chair's first question is the one that matters, and my answer is that the lattice clock is a distinct achievement. The ion clocks honoured in 2012 get their stability from one trapped quantum system. The lattice clock solves a different problem. Many neutral atoms are held in an optical lattice at the magic wavelength, where the trap leaves the clock transition unshifted, and the clock then averages over a large ensemble. That combination of long coherence and large atom number is the source of the stability gain, and it later made possible the many-body clock regime. So the citation should name the lattice and the magic wavelength explicitly, and should not name accuracy records, the frequency comb, or the redefinition of the second. This follows Lindroth's and Johansson's suggestion, and I now state it as my own condition. The consequences are real and measurable: centimetre-level relativistic geodesy, tighter limits on drifting constants and local position invariance, and ultralight dark-matter searches. Several members who ranked B051 low at the opening, Danielsson most clearly, moved toward it once they examined the physics. That supports a judgement on the science. I am treating it as that and not as a head count.
statement.case_against: The objections I cannot dismiss are three. First, lineage: the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize cover the enabling technology and the first optical clocks, and a reader may see this as a third helping of metrology. I think the physics answers this, but the citation must carry the answer. Second, attribution. Katori's proposal and first realization are clear. Ye's credit is the harder question that Olsson and the chair raised. As I understand the record, JILA's strontium lattice clock work produced the decisive accuracy, stability and systematics results, and the many-body clock followed. I am working from memory and I want an archival check on whether that is credit for invention or for an excellent later realization. If the check said Ye's contribution was refinement only, a Katori-only or differently composed prize would deserve discussion. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened. I do not think the committee should wait for it. The prize is for the demonstrated measurement capability, and that capability is established. The redefinition is an application that depends on metrology-community decisions, not on whether the physics is sound. Waiting would be a reasonable choice only if the committee wanted the application as part of the case, and I do not.

responses.point: Danielsson has moved B051 from eighth to a second part beside IceCube, accepts that lattice clocks are distinct from the earlier clock prizes, but still wants an expert report on priority and on the comb and ion overlap.
responses.response: I am glad the independent-confirmation argument reached him, and I support his request for an expert check of the lattice-clock priority record before the vote. Where I disagree is on pairing B051 with B009. His own case_against says that two unrelated parts may look like a convenience compromise, and I share that worry. A second part should be added because it is the second most compelling achievement on its own merits, not to make a three-person prize, and B009 is not yet in that position for me. Pairing would also pull the discussion away from the two things that must be settled for B051, namely the credit and the citation wording. If the IceCube credit question is resolved I will look at it again, but I am not moving on the pairing.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, prefers B051 together with B009 (Halzen alone), and says he cannot resolve the single-name credit for a large collaboration from the supplied material and may be a stronger advocate than a neutral reader.
responses.response: I appreciate that he stated his own distance from neutrality. I take his point that instrument-driven discovery is a good criterion, but the criterion only helps if the credited name matches the instrument's actual origin. A single name for a detector with hundreds of authors, with DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA as precursors, is hard to defend, and a citation limited to the 2013 diffuse flux would still need to say who made that observation possible. Without that I would not vote for it. Adding Halzen would also put a different physics community in charge of the second half of the prize. So I keep B009 off my configuration. I would not oppose it as a second part if the committee obtained an expert report that supports the credit. For my vote, B051 stands alone.

responses.point: Lindroth treats the lattice clock as a distinct achievement from ion clocks, wants the citation to name the lattice and magic-wavelength concept, and would not extend credit to Lemonde or later JILA and NIST contributors without a strong archival reason.
responses.response: I agree with the citation point and have rewritten my wording to name the lattice and the magic wavelength. On Lemonde and others I am closer to her than my round-1 uncertainty suggested, and I accept that a three-name credit would need a clear archival finding that someone else's proposal came before Katori's. I still want that check before we vote. We are both atomic physicists and, as she said, we may be too fond of this type of result. So I rely on the independent confirmation, which is outside our fields' tastes, and I take Danielsson's move as evidence that someone who did not share this taste found the case persuasive.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B027, argues that my own measurement criterion also applies to quantum-gas microscopy, and says B051 rests on a quantitative improvement of a known instrument class.
responses.response: The argument that single-site readout of correlations is a new measurement capability is fair, and it is the best reason to treat B027 as a serious candidate. I still see a difference in kind. For the clock, the new capability is the removal of a specific systematic error, and the result is checked against another independent clock at a precision of 1e-18. In B027 the credit has to be divided among five names, which he himself calls a judgement rather than settled history, and Jaksch is missing. I disagree that B051 is a purely quantitative improvement of a known instrument. A neutral-atom ensemble with no trap shift is a new design of clock, and its improved stability comes from that design. But I accept that his attribution objection to B027 and my attribution question for B051 are both about priority, and that experts should look at both.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B050 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp), calls B051 a good second choice with an incremental-precision flavour, and accepts that the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang omission is awkward.
responses.response: I do not regard B051 as incremental precision. I accept that a prize without a new state of matter has a different flavour. My difficulty with B050 is still the credit. Molenkamp's experiment tested a proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and I would not support a prize that leaves the theorists who identified HgTe uncredited unless condensed-matter members tell me Kane and Mele's Z2 classification is decisive on its own. He and the chair both say the credit question is open, so I keep B050 as my first alternative and not my preferred part. If the committee's expert report resolves the credit in favour of the three names, I would regard B050 as a close competitor to B051. I would also want to know whether the 2016 prize makes it look like a repeat. Three people on B050 would make a B050 plus B051 prize impossible, so he and I will have to choose.

uncertainties: Whether the archival record supports Ye as an inventor of the lattice clock or mainly as the leader of the accuracy and many-body-clock results; I am relying on memory.
Whether the 2001-2003 magic-wavelength proposals, including Lemonde's, precede or share priority with Katori in a way that would require a third name or change the citation.
Whether the committee will read lattice clocks as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I believe so, but it is a judgement and not a measurement.
Whether the unfinished SI redefinition should delay a prize; I do not think so, but I know others disagree.

How much weight to give B050 credit questions (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) that I cannot judge from outside condensed matter, and whether Ye's role in other atomic-physics work, such as cold molecules, should affect a single prize.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my earlier disclosure. I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye. My PhD included a stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder and JILA is Ye's institution. I consider this a distant mentor link and do not think it requires recusal, but I state it again in case colleagues disagree. I also mention that Lindroth and I share a precision-measurement background, which I regard as a bias risk and not a conflict. My subject area (rare-earth quantum memories, slow-light filters) is adjacent to B033 and B038, which are my second alternative and a candidate Johansson would recuse from, and I have no personal tie to their credited names. My WACQT role is an institutional link to Chalmers and to Johansson and does not concern B051.
